quiz_met8:1.q: A calf carries a mutation that inactivates myostatin, a growth factor that limits muscle development, and it is steadily adding muscle mass. Which of the following describes its nitrogen balance?
quiz_met8:1.r: Positive nitrogen balance means intake exceeds excretion, and it occurs during growth or recovery from injury (p. 877). The opening slide asks this about a myostatin-deficient whippet without printing the answer (p. 873).

quiz_met8:10.q: Cultured cells are depleted of ATP. Which of these steps is directly blocked because its enzyme must first phosphorylate the substrate?
quiz_met8:10.r: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP to form the intermediate gamma-glutamyl phosphate from glutamate, then swaps the phosphate for NH3 to give glutamine (p. 891). Glutaminase needs only water, the aminotransferases need glutamate, and glutamate decarboxylase needs PLP.

quiz_met8:11.q: A drug blocks enzymes that use glutamine as an amino group donor. Synthesis of which products is most directly impaired?
quiz_met8:11.r: Glutamine feeds purine and pyrimidine synthesis (pyrimidines through carbamoyl phosphate and orotic acid), and it is the primary amino group donor for biosynthetic pathways other than amino acid synthesis (p. 890, p. 899).

quiz_met8:12.q: Glutamine synthetase activity falls when a downstream product of glutamine accumulates. Which of the following is among its feedback inhibitors?
quiz_met8:12.r: The eight feedback inhibitors drawn are glycine, alanine, AMP, CTP, tryptophan, histidine, carbamoyl phosphate and glucosamine 6-phosphate, acting by concerted feedback inhibition (p. 892). Gamma-glutamyl phosphate is the reaction intermediate, not an inhibitor (p. 891).

quiz_met8:13.q: Cells are moved to a glutamine-rich medium, and the amount of glutamine synthetase protein falls. By what mechanism does glutamine lower its own synthesis?
quiz_met8:13.r: Glutamine negatively regulates its own synthesis through ubiquitylation and degradation of glutamine synthetase. Concerted feedback inhibition is the separate mechanism used by multiple downstream products (p. 892).

quiz_met8:14.q: A cell cannot carry out epigenetic modification, make creatine or convert norepinephrine to epinephrine because it lacks the universal methyl donor. Which pair reacts to form that donor? THF is tetrahydrofolate.
quiz_met8:14.r: Methionine is activated by ATP to generate S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl-group donor (p. 887), used in epigenetic modification and in synthesis of lipids, creatine and neurotransmitters (p. 886). Homocysteine plus methyl-THF makes methionine, not SAM.

quiz_met8:15.q: In vitamin B12 deficiency, methionine synthase stalls. Which compound normally hands its methyl group to homocysteine in this reaction? THF is tetrahydrofolate.
quiz_met8:15.r: Vitamin-B12-dependent methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from methyl-THF to homocysteine, producing free THF and methionine (p. 887).

quiz_met8:16.q: A patient carries a variant that lowers MTHFR activity. Which conversion is slowed? THF is tetrahydrofolate.
quiz_met8:16.r: Methyl-THF is generated by the reduction of methylene-THF by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR). Free THF to methylene-THF uses serine, and methyl-THF to free THF is methionine synthase (p. 887).

quiz_met8:17.q: Cells are given serine labeled on the carbon that it passes to the folate cycle. Which folate form first carries the label, and which amino acid is left behind? THF is tetrahydrofolate.
quiz_met8:17.r: Free THF accepts a carbon unit from serine to form methylene-THF and glycine. Methyl-THF is made only afterwards, by MTHFR (p. 887).

quiz_met8:18.q: A strict vegan of many years has megaloblastic anemia and a raised blood level of methylmalonic acid. Impairment of which enzyme accounts for the methylmalonic acid?
quiz_met8:18.r: Cobalamin (B12) is required for two enzymes. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase impairment causes accumulation of the toxic intermediate methylmalonic acid, while methionine synthase impairment causes the megaloblastic anemia (p. 888).

quiz_met8:19.q: A woman stopped eating fresh leafy green vegetables four months ago and now has megaloblastic anemia. Her methylmalonic acid level is normal. Which vitamin is most likely deficient?
quiz_met8:19.r: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, its primary risk factor is a lack of fresh leafy green vegetables, and the body stores only a 3 to 4 month supply. Methylmalonic acid accumulates in cobalamin deficiency, not folate deficiency (p. 888).

quiz_met8:2.q: A hospital pharmacy is compounding an amino acid mixture for a healthy adult. Which of the following cannot be made by the body and so must be included?
quiz_met8:2.r: Threonine is one of the nine amino acids in her essential column (Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Leu, Lys). Tyrosine, arginine, asparagine and glycine sit in her conditionally non-essential column. The slide prints the mnemonic as PVT TIM H(A)LL: the bracketed A is not in her essential column (in the usual mnemonic it stands for arginine, which she lists as conditionally non-essential) (p. 878).

quiz_met8:20.q: A cell line that can neither make nor import one amino acid cannot form 5-aminolevulinic acid despite ample succinyl-CoA. Which amino acid is missing?
quiz_met8:20.r: ALA synthase condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA to make 5-aminolevulinic acid, the first step of porphyrin (heme) synthesis (p. 894).

quiz_met8:21.q: A man taking isoniazid for tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy and a microcytic anemia. Which enzyme of heme synthesis has lost its cofactor? ALA is 5-aminolevulinic acid, PBG is porphobilinogen and PPG is protoporphyrinogen.
quiz_met8:21.r: ALA synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6) (p. 894). Isoniazid interferes with B6 metabolism, and B6 deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and a microcytic anemia because PLP is essential for heme synthesis (p. 896).

quiz_met8:22.q: A toddler living in a house with peeling old paint has an elevated blood lead level. Which two enzymes of heme synthesis does lead inhibit? ALA is 5-aminolevulinic acid, PBG is porphobilinogen and UPG is uroporphyrinogen.
quiz_met8:22.r: Lead is drawn as an inhibitor at two steps: ALA dehydratase (ALA to porphobilinogen) and ferrochelatase (iron into protoporphyrin IX to give heme) (p. 894).

quiz_met8:23.q: A 26-year-old woman has repeated attacks of severe abdominal pain with paranoia, and her urine during attacks is the color of port wine. Her father had the same attacks. Which enzyme is deficient? ALA is 5-aminolevulinic acid, PBG is porphobilinogen and UPG is uroporphyrinogen.
quiz_met8:23.r: Acute intermittent porphyria is written beside PBG deaminase (porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane): autosomal dominant, paranoia, abdominal pain, port-wine urine (p. 894).

quiz_met8:24.q: A 50-year-old man who drinks heavily has blisters and hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed skin and red-brown urine. Which intermediate is the substrate of his deficient enzyme?
quiz_met8:24.r: Porphyria cutanea tarda is written beside UPG III decarboxylase, which converts uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III: most common, autosomal dominant, photosensitivity with blisters and hyperpigmentation, red-brown urine, exacerbated by alcohol (p. 894).

quiz_met8:25.q: A child lacks aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. Which two neurotransmitters are made directly by this enzyme and so are deficient?
quiz_met8:25.r: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (with PLP) converts dopa to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. GABA is made by glutamate decarboxylase and histamine by histidine decarboxylase (p. 895).

quiz_met8:26.q: A newborn cannot regenerate tetrahydrobiopterin. Which step of neurotransmitter synthesis fails for lack of this cofactor?
quiz_met8:26.r: Tyrosine hydroxylase (tyrosine to dopa) and tryptophan hydroxylase use tetrahydrobiopterin. Dopa to dopamine and glutamate to GABA use PLP, dopamine to norepinephrine uses ascorbate, and norepinephrine to epinephrine uses adoMet (p. 895).

quiz_met8:27.q: A patient is placed on a diet very low in tryptophan. Besides serotonin, which two products of tryptophan are expected to fall?
quiz_met8:27.r: Tryptophan gives serotonin, which goes on to melatonin, and tryptophan also gives niacin. Melanin comes from dopa (tyrosine) through tyrosinase, histamine from histidine and GABA from glutamate (p. 895).

quiz_met8:28.q: A patient lacks the amidinotransferase that makes guanidinoacetate, the immediate precursor of creatine. Which two amino acids are this enzyme's substrates?
quiz_met8:28.r: Amidinotransferase combines glycine and arginine to give guanidinoacetate plus ornithine. A methyltransferase then adds a methyl group from adoMet (methionine) to give creatine (p. 897).

quiz_met8:29.q: Hepatocytes build carnitine from a trimethylated amino acid that is released by protein degradation. Which amino acid is trimethylated in this starting material?
quiz_met8:29.r: Carnitine synthesis starts from N6-trimethyllysine (TML) released by protein degradation, then runs through HTML, TMABA and gamma-butyrobetaine to carnitine (p. 897).

quiz_met8:3.q: A previously healthy man is admitted with severe burns. In the lecture's classification, the need for which amino acid spikes in this setting, although the body normally makes enough of it?
quiz_met8:3.r: Proline is in the conditionally non-essential column (Arg, Asn, Gln, Gly, Pro, Ser, Tyr), whose need spikes in severe trauma, burns, major surgery, critical illness, rapid growth and intense training. Alanine, aspartate, cysteine and glutamate are in her plain non-essential column (p. 878).

quiz_met8:30.q: The body's most common thiol antioxidant is a tripeptide assembled in two ATP-dependent steps. Which three amino acids form it?
quiz_met8:30.r: Glutamate-cysteine ligase joins glutamate and cysteine, then glutathione synthase adds glycine, each step using ATP. Glutathione is the most common thiol antioxidant and needs NADPH to be recycled to its reduced form (p. 898).

quiz_met8:4.q: A 3-year-old has pitting edema, a fatty liver and hair changes with a flag sign. A dietary recall shows that total calorie intake is adequate. Which dietary deficit explains this picture?
quiz_met8:4.r: Kwashiorkor results from prolonged deficiency in protein intake, not from an overall lack of calories. A total calorie deficit is marasmus (p. 880).

quiz_met8:5.q: A 5-year-old whose diet is almost entirely bread and potato chips has pitting edema, an enlarged liver and pale, easily pluckable hair. Which blood value is expected to be reduced?
quiz_met8:5.r: Kwashiorkor bloodwork shows normal to high non-essential amino acids but a severe reduction in essential amino acids and urea (p. 880). This is the lecture's own case question (p. 874).

quiz_met8:6.q: Plasma amino acids are measured in a child with kwashiorkor. Which pair is most likely to be severely reduced?
quiz_met8:6.r: Essential amino acids are severely reduced in kwashiorkor, while non-essential ones are normal to high (p. 880). Leucine and lysine are both on the essential list (p. 878).

quiz_met8:7.q: Hepatocytes convert pyruvate to alanine. Which molecule directly donates the amino group in this reaction?
quiz_met8:7.r: Alpha amino groups come from glutamate during amino acid synthesis: alanine aminotransferase moves the amino group of glutamate onto pyruvate, leaving alpha-ketoglutarate (p. 883, p. 884). Glutamine supplies most other amino groups.

quiz_met8:8.q: A cell line cannot convert 3-phosphoglycerate into its amino acid product. By the lecture's list of origins of non-essential amino acids, synthesis of which two further amino acids is lost as a result?
quiz_met8:8.r: Serine comes from 3-phosphoglycerate, glycine comes from serine, and cysteine comes from serine with its sulfur from methionine (p. 882).

quiz_met8:9.q: An infant formula is made without phenylalanine. Which amino acid, normally made by the body, can no longer be synthesized?
quiz_met8:9.r: Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, an essential amino acid (p. 882, p. 884). Cysteine depends on methionine for its sulfur, not on phenylalanine.

brief:
Met 8: Amino Acid Metabolism (Jones) high-yield tables

Source: lecture slides, PDF pages 872 to 899. Every table cites its PDF page.

Note on acronyms: the slides spell out SAM, SAH, MS, THF, MTHFR and PLP. They never spell out ATP, ADP, AMP, CTP, GTP, NAD, NADPH, FAD, TCA, CoA, GABA, CBS, TB, GI, adoMet, adoHcy, BCAA, BCKA, SSA, or the enzyme labels ALAT, AAT, BCAT, GDH, PAG, GS, GAD, GABA-T, SSADH, TMLD, HTMLA, TMABA DH and BBD. Their expansions below are standard names (outside the slides).

1. Nitrogen balance and essential amino acids (LO 1)

Nitrogen balance is the difference between nitrogen (protein) intake and excretion, and nine amino acids must come from the diet (p. 877, p. 878).

Table 1a. The three states of nitrogen balance (p. 877)

State Definition When it happens

Positive Intake exceeds excretion Recovery from injury
Neutral Intake equals excretion Normal situation for many healthy adults
Negative Excretion exceeds intake Weight loss
Negative Excretion exceeds intake Starvation
Negative Excretion exceeds intake Ketoacidosis

Table 1b. The nitrogen pool (p. 877)

Connected to the amino acid pool Direction of the arrow
Dietary protein In only
Tissue protein, plasma protein, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, hemoglobin Both ways
Other new amino acids Both ways
Non-protein compounds: heme, heterocyclic amines Both ways
Glucose, glycogen, lipids Out only
Catabolism: carbon dioxide, water, urea, energy Out only

2. Kwashiorkor (LO 2)

3. Glutamate and synthesis of non-essential amino acids (LO 3)

4. Glutamine (LO 4)

Glycine builds porphyrins, tyrosine, tryptophan, glutamate and histidine build neurotransmitters, and small sets of amino acids build creatine, carnitine and glutathione (p. 894 to p. 898).
